paper.title: Deep Batch Active Learning by Diverse, Uncertain Gradient Lower Bounds
paper.authors: Jordan T. Ash (Princeton University), Chicheng Zhang (University of Arizona), Akshay Krishnamurthy (Microsoft Research NYC), John Langford (Microsoft Research NYC), Alekh Agarwal (Microsoft Research Redmond)

core_method.name: BADGE: Batch Active learning by Diverse Gradient Embeddings
core_method.summary: Selects batches of unlabeled examples by computing gradient embeddings of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the last layer weights (using the model's own predicted labels as proxy labels) and applying k-MEANS++ seeding to sample diverse, high-magnitude points in this gradient space, simultaneously capturing predictive uncertainty and sample diversity without hand-tuned hyperparameters.

paper_claims.method_description: BADGE selects batches of unlabeled examples by computing gradient embeddings of the cross-entropy loss w.r.t. the last layer weights, using the model's own predicted labels as 'hallucinated' labels. It then applies k-MEANS++ seeding on these embeddings to sample diverse, high-magnitude points. Gradient magnitude captures predictive uncertainty (confident examples have small gradient norms) while k-MEANS++ spread ensures diversity, solving the fundamental failure mode of pure uncertainty sampling where top-K uncertain examples are near-duplicates.
paper_claims.claimed_results: BADGE consistently performs as well as or better than the best baseline across 231 experiments (7 datasets x 3 architectures x 3 batch sizes x 5 repeats). It beats CORESET on datasets where penultimate-layer features lack meaningful geometry, beats uncertainty-based methods when batch sizes are large, and outperforms the ALBL meta-algorithm. The key contribution is robustness across architecture, batch size, and dataset without any hand-tuned hyperparameters.
paper_claims.benchmark_scale: 7 datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN + 4 OpenML tabular datasets #6/#155/#156/#184), 3 architectures (2-layer MLP, ResNet-18, VGG-11), 3 batch sizes (100, 1000, 10000), initial labeled set M=100, trained with Adam until >99% training accuracy, 5 random seeds per configuration.

try_it_out.definition: Try BADGE by running a batch active learning cycle: given a trained classifier and an unlabeled data pool, BADGE computes per-sample gradient embeddings and uses k-MEANS++ seeding to select a batch of diverse, uncertain examples for labeling. Watching the learning curve improve across rounds demonstrates the algorithm's effectiveness.

user_provides.name: Classification dataset
user_provides.description: A labeled dataset with feature vectors x_pool (N_pool, n_features) and integer labels y_pool (N_pool,). MNIST is the default demo dataset.

user_provides.name: Model architecture
user_provides.description: A neural network classifier with a softmax output layer and an exposed penultimate layer (for gradient embedding computation). The paper's 2-layer MLP is the default.

system_provides.name: select_batch acquisition function
system_provides.description: The complete BADGE acquisition function: per-sample gradient embedding computation (Equation 1), k-MEANS++ seeding (Algorithm 2), and batch index selection.

system_provides.name: Active learning training loop
system_provides.description: Bootstrap initialization (M random labels), per-round model retraining from scratch, acquisition, and test accuracy evaluation.

data_requirements.format: Tensors: x_pool (N_pool, n_features) feature vectors, y_pool (N_pool,) integer labels in [0, n_classes-1]. For image data with MLP, images are flattened to 1D vectors (e.g., MNIST 28x28 -> 784). For CNNs, images retain their 4D shape (B, C, H, W). For tabular OpenML data, features are raw numeric vectors.
data_requirements.auto_download_details: MNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN available via torchvision.datasets. OpenML datasets available programmatically via skopenml.
data_requirements.synthetic_description: Can generate synthetic 2D classification data (e.g., concentric circles, two moons, or multiclass Gaussian blobs) for quick MLP demos on small pools.

dependencies.estimated_time: Minutes for smoke-scale demo (MLP on MNIST, small pool, ~10 rounds)

classification.detection_reasoning: BADGE is the canonical reference method for the batch active acquisition paradigm. It selects multiple examples per round (B=100/1000/10000) using gradient embeddings and k-MEANS++ seeding, directly addressing the uncertainty-versus-diversity trade-off that defines batch AL.

comparison.description: The paper compares BADGE against 6 baselines (CORESET, Confidence, Margin, Entropy, ALBL, Random) across 33 dataset-architecture-batch_size combinations. The independent variable is the acquisition strategy; all methods share the same model architecture, training protocol (Adam, retrain from scratch until >99% accuracy), dataset, initial labeled set (M=100), and batch size. Results are aggregated via pairwise penalty matrices and normalized-error CDFs.

pluggable_component.name: select_batch
pluggable_component.description: The BADGE acquisition function. Computes gradient embeddings for all unlabeled candidates using the model's predicted labels and last-layer weights, then selects batch_size diverse, high-magnitude samples via k-MEANS++ seeding. Returns indices into x_unlabeled. The only stochastic component is k-MEANS++'s initial centroid selection, controlled by seed. No extra parameters are needed beyond these arguments.

controlled_variables.model_architecture: Same architecture class (MLP/ResNet/VGG) across all methods in a given experiment
controlled_variables.training_protocol: Retrain from scratch each round using Adam until >99% training accuracy; no warm-starting
controlled_variables.label_budget: Same initial labeled set size (M=100) and batch size B across methods
controlled_variables.unlabeled_pool: Same pool of unlabeled examples U available for selection across methods
controlled_variables.data_preprocessing: Identical preprocessing and normalization across all methods

comparison.independent_variable: Batch acquisition strategy (BADGE vs. CORESET vs. Confidence vs. Margin vs. Entropy vs. ALBL vs. Random)
comparison.evaluation_checkpoints: Test accuracy evaluated after the initial labeled set and after each acquisition round, producing a learning curve of accuracy vs. total labeled samples queried.
comparison.primary_metric: Test accuracy (1 - 0/1 error) on the held-out test set
comparison.visualization: Learning curves (accuracy vs. #labels queried), pairwise penalty matrices over all (dataset, architecture, batch_size) combinations, and CDFs of normalized errors relative to the Random baseline

model.architecture: Neural network classifier with a softmax output layer. The paper uses a 2-layer MLP with ReLU (hidden dim 256 for image data, 1024 for OpenML tabular data), an 18-layer ResNet, or an 11-layer VGG. For MNIST only MLP is used since the dataset is too easy for CNNs to differentiate methods.

specific_features.why_essential: The gradient embedding formula (Equation 1) is derived assuming softmax activation at the output. Proposition 1 (gradient norm lower bound) and the analytical embedding computation both require the softmax parametrization.

specific_features.feature: Penultimate layer output accessible via forward_with_embedding hook
specific_features.why_essential: Gradient embedding computation (Equation 1: (g_x)_i = (p_i - I(y_hat==i)) * z) requires z(x;V), the penultimate layer output. Without access to z, the embedding cannot be computed analytically and would require per-sample autograd backpropagation.
The gradient embedding is defined as the gradient of the cross-entropy loss w.r.t. last layer weights. A different loss function would produce a fundamentally different embedding space.
The paper's MLP uses ReLU activations. While the gradient embedding formula works with any penultimate output, the paper's specific results assume ReLU.

training.learning_rate: 0.001 for image data (MNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN), 0.0001 for non-image (OpenML) data

blockers.requirement: Penultimate layer output for analytical gradient embedding computation
blockers.reason: The model architecture must expose forward_with_embedding (or equivalent) to provide z(x;V) so gradient embeddings can be computed analytically via Equation 1 rather than requiring per-sample autograd.
blockers.resolution: Implement forward_with_embedding(self, x: Tensor) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor] on the architecture class, returning (logits, penultimate_z).

blockers.requirement: Retrain from scratch each acquisition round (no warm-starting)
blockers.reason: The paper explicitly avoids warm-starting (citing Ash and Adams, 2019) and builds a fresh model each round. Warm-starting changes the optimization trajectory and affects acquisition quality.
blockers.resolution: The acquisition loop must call build_model() to create a fresh model with independent random initialization at the start of each round, then train_from_scratch on the current labeled set.

required_model_methods.name: forward_with_embedding
required_model_methods.returns_description: Tuple of (logits, penultimate_embedding) where logits is the pre-softmax output from the final linear layer, shape (B, n_classes), and penultimate_embedding is the activation from the layer immediately before the classifier head, shape (B, hidden_dim). For an MLP, this is the output of the hidden ReLU layer.
required_model_methods.purpose: Gradient embedding computation (Equation 1) requires z(x;V), the penultimate layer output. For each sample n and class i: (g_n)_i = (p_ni - I(y_hat_n==i)) * z_n, producing the full K*d gradient embedding. This hook avoids per-sample autograd backpropagation.
required_model_methods.called_from: method/method.py within compute_gradient_embeddings: pass all unlabeled candidates through forward_with_embedding to get penultimate outputs and logits before computing gradient embeddings analytically.

elements.paper_evidence: The hallucinated-label gradient embedding g_x computed as (g_x)_i = (p_i - I(y_hat==i)) * z(x;V) across K class blocks of dimension d is the fundamental representation BADGE uses. Proposition 1 proves this embedding lower-bounds the true gradient for any label.
elements.technical_concept: Last-layer gradient embedding with hallucinated label
elements.required_behavior: For each unlabeled candidate, compute the model's predicted label y_hat (argmax of softmax output), then compute the gradient of the cross-entropy loss w.r.t. the last layer weight matrix W (shape K*d) using y_hat as the label. The result is a flattened K*d vector per sample.
elements.demo_scale_implementation: Use forward_with_embedding to obtain logits and penultimate z for all candidates. Compute softmax probabilities, identify y_hat per sample, then compute embeddings analytically: for class i, block_i = (p_i - I(y_hat==i)) * z, flattened to (N_candidates, K*d).
forbidden_substitutions: Do not replace gradient embeddings with penultimate layer features alone (as CORESET does)
Do not use MC dropout, ensembles, or Bayesian uncertainty estimation; BADGE is purely deterministic gradient-based
Do not compute gradients w.r.t. all network parameters; Proposition 1 only holds for last-layer gradients
Do not use a different proxy label (e.g., uniformly random, or all K labels aggregated)
required_controls: Use the same trained model snapshot for all candidate gradient embedding computations within a single acquisition round
Ensure model.eval() (no dropout, no batchnorm noise) during embedding computation
fairness_checks: The gradient embedding computation must be identical across all candidates; only the input x varies
All candidates must be embedded with the same weight snapshot and same softmax parametrization
elements.feasibility_rationale: The mechanism is fully specified by Equation 1 and Algorithm 1. It can be implemented at any scale given a model with forward_with_embedding and basic tensor operations.
verification_expectations: method.py calls model.forward_with_embedding to obtain penultimate outputs for all candidates
Gradient embeddings are computed using the model's argmax softmax label, not any true labels
Embedding tensor has shape (N_candidates, K*d) where K is the number of classes and d is the hidden dimension

elements.paper_evidence: k-MEANS++ seeding on gradient embeddings selects batches that are simultaneously diverse (via distance-based sequential sampling) and high-magnitude (probability proportional to squared distance to nearest centroid). The paper explicitly replaces k-DPP with k-MEANS++ for computational tractability.
elements.required_behavior: Apply k-MEANS++ seeding to the gradient embedding vectors {g_x : x in U\S} to select exactly batch_size candidates. The first centroid is chosen uniformly at random from candidates. Each subsequent centroid is chosen with probability proportional to the squared Euclidean distance to its nearest already-chosen centroid.
elements.demo_scale_implementation: Implement k-MEANS++ seeding (Algorithm 2 from Appendix A) operating on the gradient embedding vectors of shape (N_candidates, K*d). Use the seed parameter to initialize a NumPy random generator for the uniform first-centroid selection and all subsequent probabilistic choices.
forbidden_substitutions: Do not replace k-MEANS++ with random selection, top-k by gradient magnitude, or greedy furthest-first traversal (FF-k-CENTER)
Do not use k-DPP or any alternative sampling mechanism; k-MEANS++ was specifically chosen over k-DPP for its computational efficiency and near-identical statistical performance
Do not operate k-MEANS++ in input space, penultimate-layer feature space, or any space other than the gradient embedding space
required_controls: k-MEANS++ must operate in the gradient embedding space of dimension K*d
The distance metric must be Euclidean distance in the embedding space
The seed must control all stochastic choices in k-MEANS++ (first centroid, all subsequent samples)
fairness_checks: The embedding space is derived from the same model snapshot and same last-layer-restriction across all candidates
No candidates are removed or added to the pool during k-MEANS++ seeding
elements.feasibility_rationale: k-MEANS++ seeding is a well-defined, efficiently implementable O(N*k*d) algorithm. The paper provides complete pseudocode in Appendix A. No scale-dependent hyperparameters exist.
verification_expectations: method.py implements k-MEANS++ seeding as sequential sampling matching Algorithm 2 (first centroid uniform, subsequent proportional to squared distance)
The seeding operates on gradient embeddings (shape K*d), not on raw input features or penultimate-layer activations
The seed parameter is used to initialize a reproducible random generator for k-MEANS++

elements.paper_evidence: BADGE computes gradients only w.r.t. the last (output) layer parameters theta_out = W in R^{K*d}. This restriction is essential for Proposition 1 (the lower bound proof) and keeps computation tractable (avoiding full-network backpropagation for each candidate).
elements.technical_concept: Gradient computation restricted to last layer weights only
elements.required_behavior: Gradient embedding computation targets only the last layer weight matrix W (shape K*d). The previous layer weights V (all hidden layer parameters) are not differentiated through. The embedding formula (Equation 1) inherently satisfies this restriction.
elements.demo_scale_implementation: Compute the gradient embedding analytically using z(x;V) and softmax outputs (Equation 1). This formula computes exactly the gradient w.r.t. W, with no backpropagation through V. The analytical computation is O(N*K*d) per batch.
forbidden_substitutions: Do not compute full-network gradients or backpropagate through hidden layers
elements.feasibility_rationale: The analytical formula (Equation 1) inherently computes only last-layer gradients. The implementation uses forward_with_embedding to get z, then applies the formula directly. No approximation needed.
verification_expectations: Embedding has shape K*d per sample (last layer weight dimensions), confirming restriction to last layer
No autograd backpropagation through the full network is used for embedding computation

elements.paper_evidence: The paper explicitly states: 'We avoid warm starting and retrain models from scratch every time new samples are queried (Ash and Adams, 2019).' Algorithm 1 Step 7: 'Train a model theta_{t+1} on S by minimizing E_S[CE(f(x;theta), y)].'
elements.technical_concept: Retrain model from scratch after each acquisition round
elements.required_behavior: At the start of each acquisition round, build a fresh model with independent random weight initialization and train it from scratch on the currently labeled set until training accuracy exceeds 99% (or the demo-equivalent stopping criterion).
elements.demo_scale_implementation: In the notebook acquisition loop, call build_model() to create a fresh model at each round, then train_from_scratch on x_pool[labeled_idx], y_pool[labeled_idx]. For demo scale, reduce the stop criterion (e.g., 80% training accuracy) or fix a small epoch count, but always build a new model.
forbidden_substitutions: Do not warm-start training from the previous round's model weights; this changes the optimization trajectory and acquisition quality
required_controls: Each round must produce a model with identical architecture but independent random initialization
elements.feasibility_rationale: This is a straightforward protocol: build a new model and train it each round. The paper provides clear pseudocode in Algorithm 1.
verification_expectations: The acquisition loop calls build_model() at each round to create a fresh model
No model state (weights, optimizer) is carried over from the previous round

methodology_contract_pack.summary: The demo must preserve BADGE's core dual mechanism: computing per-sample last-layer gradient embeddings with hallucinated labels, and selecting batches via k-MEANS++ seeding in that gradient space.
implementation_obligations: For each unlabeled candidate, compute the gradient of CE loss w.r.t. last layer weights using the model's predicted label (argmax of softmax output) as a proxy label.
Apply k-MEANS++ seeding on the resulting gradient embedding vectors to select batch_size diverse, high-magnitude samples.
Operate k-MEANS++ in the gradient embedding space (K*d dimensions), not in input space or penultimate-layer space.
Retrain the model from scratch at the start of each acquisition round.
forbidden_substitutions: Do not replace gradient embeddings with penultimate layer features alone (as CORESET does).
Do not replace k-MEANS++ with random selection, top-k magnitude, or greedy furthest-first traversal.
Do not use MC dropout, ensembles, or Bayesian uncertainty; BADGE is purely deterministic gradient-based.
Do not warm-start training from the previous round's model weights.
Do not compute full-network gradients; BADGE targets only last-layer weights.
required_controls: Use the same trained model snapshot for all candidate gradient embeddings within a single round.
k-MEANS++ must operate in the gradient embedding space of dimension K*d.
Each round must produce a model with identical architecture but independent initialization.
verification_expectations: method.py calls model.forward_with_embedding to obtain penultimate outputs for all candidates.
Gradient embeddings use the model's argmax label (not true labels) and have shape (N_candidates, K*d).
method.py implements k-MEANS++ seeding as sequential sampling matching Algorithm 2 from the paper.
The acquisition loop creates a fresh model at each round with no weight carryover.
